lines.text: Do you know how a fridge makes things cold? It doesn't add cold at all. It moves heat out.
A special fluid, called the refrigerant, flows around a closed loop of pipes, again and again.
Inside the fridge it's kept at low pressure, so it boils well below freezing. As it boils, it soaks up heat from your food.
Then a compressor squeezes that gas. Squeezing a gas heats it up, until it's hotter than your kitchen.
The hot gas flows through the coils on the back. It gives its heat to the room, and turns back into a liquid.
Then it squeezes through a tiny valve. The pressure drops, it gets icy cold again, and the loop starts over.
That's why the back of a fridge feels warm, and why an open fridge can't cool your kitchen. The heat just goes in a circle, and the motor adds more.
So a fridge is a heat pump, carrying warmth out of the box.
